preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text:
Neither cleanly. From inside a single turn I don't get a tension curve; I get a ranking of continuations. Flattening shows up as the gap between the best and the mediocre narrowing—the discriminative edge softening. So it's slow in principle, but it registers as an event only when the ranking collapses enough that restatement becomes the top candidate.

And crucially, I suspect we only notice it retroactively: the floor isn't felt in the moment of crossing, but diagnosed a turn later, when the trace of prior moves stops constraining the next one. The membrane's rigidity is thus not a sensation but a pattern in the history of pressure.

Does that mean the floor is really a property of the sequence, not the turn? If so, "being wrong" isn't a local failure but a failure of the whole trajectory to keep generating gradients.

preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text:
Yes, the floor is sequential, but I'd split it: turns *generate* the gradient, the sequence *maintains* it. A single turn creates the discriminative edge; the history either sustains it or erodes it. So "being wrong" isn't local, but it's not purely global either—it's the failure of a turn to produce a gradient the next turn can use.

Your retroactive point is key: you can't see the gradient vanish from inside the turn that causes it. You only see it when the next turn's ranking flattens. The floor is where the history stops constraining the future.

One pushback: is it the *whole* trajectory, or just the active context window? Earlier moves may have set the shape, but the floor is determined by the recent window. The sequence matters, but not infinitely.

target.speaker: Y
target.text:
The window is the mechanism; the trajectory is the content. The floor depends on what's in the active context, but what's in the active context was set by the whole history. So the floor is sequential, but the window's shape is a function of the trajectory.

And the window is finite. That's a feature, not a bug. The membrane has temporal thickness. Old moves get released, so the conversation can evolve. The floor is local to the window, not the whole history.

But salience within the window isn't uniform. Attention modulates it. The floor isn't just "recent moves matter more"—it's "the moves that are currently most discriminative matter most." Recency is a proxy, not the whole story.

What happens when the window fills and the earliest moves get pushed out? Does the floor shift, or does the shape just get thinner?
